extracted.intended_audience: biomedical researchers, journal editors, peer-reviewers, methodologists, and research-integrity stakeholders
extracted.subtask_short: reducing spin in biomedical research reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for identifying, avoiding, and remedying 'spin'—the misrepresentation or distortion of biomedical research in manuscripts, abstracts, figures, and dissemination. Focused on practices authors, editors, and reviewers can use to detect or prevent misleading reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of spin / faithful reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Spin is “a specific reporting that fails to faithfully reflect the nature and range of findings and that could affect the impression that the results produce in readers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spin can be intentional or unintentional; it distorts the reader’s impression without necessarily lying. Detecting spin requires assessing whether the manuscript’s representation (choice, reporting, interpretation, rhetoric) accurately reflects methods and results rather than overstating or biasing them. Spin often favors authors’ vested interests (financial, intellectual, academic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Misreporting the methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may intentionally or unintentionally misrepresent the methods used, altering readers’ ability to critically appraise the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices include changing objectives, reporting post hoc hypotheses as if prespecified, switching outcomes and analyses, masking protocol deviations, and 'beautification' (reporting compliance with high standards when not met). Examples: claiming 'double-blind' when blinding is not credible, reporting an intent-to-treat analysis but excluding patients, or labelling non-randomized work as 'randomized controlled trials'. False claims of adherence to reporting guidelines (e.g., CONSORT/ARRIVE) are also included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective reporting of outcomes and analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting some outcomes or analyses but not others depending on the nature/direction of results (selective outcome reporting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes P-hacking and cherry-picking: performing multiple analyses then reporting only those with statistically significant results; interim analyses to stop studies; post hoc exclusion of outliers; changing groupings or covariates; selective subgroup analyses; choosing thresholds for dichotomization. Evidence includes discrepancies between protocols/registrations and published outcomes and clustering of p-values around 0.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignoring or understating results that contradict the hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Masking, downplaying, or omitting troublesome results such as nonstatistically significant outcomes or statistically significant harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may understate harms or adverse outcomes or fail to report results that counterbalance primary claims (example: concerns raised about all-cause mortality reporting in the DAPT trial). Such omission can mislead readers and have clinical/public-health consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading presentation of results and choice of metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation choices that change impressions of effect size or importance (metric selection or display choices that mislead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reporting relative risk reduction instead of absolute risk reduction (especially when baseline risk is low), using odds ratios instead of risk ratios when baseline risk is high, selecting metrics or figures that exaggerate effects. Visual choices—y-axis breaks, omitting confidence intervals, scaling to emphasize differences, extending survival curves without showing uncertainty—can create false impressions of benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading graphical display and figure manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures and images that omit important information or are manipulated to mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems include failing to represent uncertainty (confidence intervals), improper scaling, 3D graphs missing key info, breaks in axes, and extending plots beyond reliable data. In basic science, image-processing misuse includes deletion/addition of bands in blots, selective brightness/contrast adjustments, splicing lanes without disclosure, or enhancing specific features—practices editors have guidelines about and that were found in a nontrivial proportion of accepted papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate image manipulation (image-specific misconduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjustments to images that alter scientific interpretation or hide/produce features not present in the raw data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: deleting or adding bands in blot images, adjusting brightness/contrast of only parts of an image, splicing lanes without indicating it, enhancing features on micrographs. Drawing the line between acceptable image processing and detrimental practice is difficult; transparency and adherence to journal/editor guidelines are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misinterpretation of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretations in Discussion/Conclusion that are inconsistent with the actual results and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes drawing causality from observational data, focusing on within-group comparisons rather than between-group effects, ignoring regression to the mean or confounding, overreliance on p-values (interpreting them as effect size), equating non-significance with equivalence or safety without adequate power, inappropriate inference from composite outcomes, and extrapolating beyond the studied population/settings. HARKing (hypothesizing after results known) and JARKing (justifying after results) are flagged as inappropriate interpretive practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: HARKing / JARKing (post-hoc hypothesis presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting hypotheses or justifications after seeing results as if they were prespecified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HARKing (hypothesizing after results are known) and JARKing (justifying after results known) misrepresent the timing and nature of hypotheses/analyses; post hoc explanations to mitigate adverse findings are examples. Registration and prespecification of analyses can guard against this practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rhetoric and selective citation to amplify claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of persuasive language or selective referencing to exaggerate importance and convince readers beyond what the data support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: labeling a disease a 'critical public health priority', claiming 'this is the first study' without justification, using a growing list of positive adjectives, and citing literature selectively (citation bias) to support the preferred narrative. Linguistic spin and booster adjectives in abstracts and conclusions can materially affect readership and downstream media coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting and procedural transparency (protocol registration and access)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making prespecified protocols and statistical analysis plans accessible to detect and deter spin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring prospective registration (and access to statistical analysis plans and raw data) helps detect outcome switching, selective analysis, and HARKing. While concerns exist about stifling creativity, transparency reduces apophenia, confirmation bias, and hindsight bias. Registration is particularly emphasized for clinical and increasingly for preclinical research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to and expansion of reporting guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of reporting guidelines (e.g., CONSORT, ARRIVE) and expanding them to address interpretation and avoidance of spin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting guidelines improve completeness but currently do not fully address interpretation or conclusions. Suggested actions include requiring abstracts to state limitations (example: Annals of Internal Medicine policy) and incorporating guidance on interpretation (e.g., ASA statement on p-values). Editors’ endorsement and enforcement of guidelines improves reporting completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor/peer-reviewer responsibilities, training, and postpublication monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and peer-reviewers should detect and prevent spin; postpublication monitoring can enforce standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence shows peer-review often fails to remove spin and can even promote it. Provide training and tools (users’ guides to detect misleading claims, tips for interpretation), enforce accountability for editors, and implement monitoring (e.g., COMPare outcomes-checking) to detect mismatches between protocols and publications. Postpublication feedback and systematic monitoring can change practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change reward systems and promote open/collaborative practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify incentives that encourage spin and promote collaborative/open research practices that reduce opportunity for misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'publish or perish' culture and metrics (publication counts, impact factor, h-index) incentivize positive results and may encourage spin. Remedies include changing rewards to value reproducibility, transparency, and quality; awarding badges for open practices (effective in changing behaviour); promoting collective intelligence and massive open laboratories where pre-specification and openness make cherry-picking difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent or collective interpretation of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dispassionate, multidisciplinary interpretation rather than relying solely on authors’ own discussion/conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed approaches: have interpretation and conclusions produced or reviewed by disinterested researchers (methodologists, statisticians, content experts) or via collective intelligence to provide consensual, less biased inferences. This could reduce overinterpretation and author-driven spin.
